claim: Rgs12 is essential for osteoclast differentiation.
source: We previously demonstrated that Rgs12 is essential for osteoclast differentiation and its deletion in vivo protected mice against pathological bone loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Rgs12 deletion in vivo protected mice against pathological bone loss.
source: We previously demonstrated that Rgs12 is essential for osteoclast differentiation and its deletion in vivo protected mice against pathological bone loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Rgs12 deletion in vivo led to an osteopetrotic phenotype evidenced by increased trabecular bone.
source: Rgs12 deletion in vivo led to an osteopetrotic phenotype evidenced by increased trabecular bone, decreased osteoclast number and activity but no change in osteoblast number and bone formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including micro-CT analysis and histological assessment.

claim: Rgs12 deletion in vivo led to decreased osteoclast number and activity.
source: Rgs12 deletion in vivo led to an osteopetrotic phenotype evidenced by increased trabecular bone, decreased osteoclast number and activity but no change in osteoblast number and bone formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including TRAP staining and bone resorption assays.

claim: Rgs12 deletion in vivo resulted in no change in osteoblast number and bone formation.
source: Rgs12 deletion in vivo led to an osteopetrotic phenotype evidenced by increased trabecular bone, decreased osteoclast number and activity but no change in osteoblast number and bone formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including histological assessment and dynamic histomorphometry.

claim: Rgs12 overexpression increased osteoclast number and size.
source: Rgs12 overexpression increased osteoclast number and size, and bone resorption activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RAW264.7 cells overexpressing Rgs12.

claim: Rgs12 overexpression increased bone resorption activity.
source: Rgs12 overexpression increased osteoclast number and size, and bone resorption activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from bone resorption assays using RAW264.7 cells overexpressing Rgs12.

claim: Proteomics analysis of Rgs12-depleted osteoclasts identified an upregulation of antioxidant enzymes under the transcriptional regulation of Nrf2.
source: Proteomics analysis of Rgs12-depleted osteoclasts identified an upregulation of antioxidant enzymes under the transcriptional regulation of Nrf2, the master regulator of oxidative stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nrf2 is the master regulator of oxidative stress.
source: Proteomics analysis of Rgs12-depleted osteoclasts identified an upregulation of antioxidant enzymes under the transcriptional regulation of Nrf2, the master regulator of oxidative stress.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Nrf2's role.

claim: There was an increase of Nrf2 activity in Rgs12-deficient cells.
source: We confirmed an increase of Nrf2 activity and impaired reactive oxygen species production in Rgs12-deficient cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including western blotting and immunofluorescence staining.

claim: There was impaired reactive oxygen species production in Rgs12-deficient cells.
source: We confirmed an increase of Nrf2 activity and impaired reactive oxygen species production in Rgs12-deficient cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using DCFDA fluorescence method to measure ROS levels.

claim: Rgs12 overexpression suppressed Nrf2 through a mechanism dependent on the 26S proteasome.
source: Conversely, Rgs12 overexpression suppressed Nrf2 through a mechanism dependent on the 26S proteasome, and promoted RANKL-induced phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and NFκB, which was abrogated by antioxidant treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using proteasome inhibitor MG-132.

claim: Rgs12 overexpression promoted RANKL-induced phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and NFκB.
source: Conversely, Rgs12 overexpression suppressed Nrf2 through a mechanism dependent on the 26S proteasome, and promoted RANKL-induced phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and NFκB, which was abrogated by antioxidant treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and NFκB.

claim: The Rgs12-mediated promotion of RANKL-induced phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and NFκB was abrogated by antioxidant treatment.
source: Conversely, Rgs12 overexpression suppressed Nrf2 through a mechanism dependent on the 26S proteasome, and promoted RANKL-induced phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and NFκB, which was abrogated by antioxidant treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using NAC as an antioxidant.

claim: Rgs12 has a novel role in regulating Nrf2, thereby controlling cellular redox state and osteoclast differentiation.
source: Our study therefore identified a novel role of Rgs12 in regulating Nrf2, thereby controlling cellular redox state and osteoclast differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Osteoporosis affects an estimated 200 million people worldwide.
source: The disease has a significant global impact, affecting an estimated 200 million people worldwide and exerts a heavy economic burden.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Amin et al., 2014.

claim: Osteoporosis disease prevalence is projected to rise by approximately 50% within the next ten years.
source: Moreover, disease prevalence is projected to rise by approximately 50% within the next ten years (Amin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Amin et al., 2014.

claim: Bone remodeling is carried out by the coordinated actions of the bone-forming osteoblasts and the bone-resorbing osteoclasts.
source: Bone remodeling is carried out by the coordinated actions of the bone-forming osteoblasts (OBs) and the bone-resorbing osteoclasts (OCs).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about bone biology.

claim: Disorders of skeletal deficiency such as osteoporosis are typically characterized by enhanced osteoclastic bone resorption relative to bone formation.
source: Disorders of skeletal deficiency such as osteoporosis are typically characterized by enhanced osteoclastic bone resorption relative to bone formation, thereby resulting in net bone loss.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about osteoporosis pathophysiology.

claim: RGS proteins play a classical role in attenuating G protein-coupled receptor signaling through its GTPase-accelerating protein activity to inactivate the Gα subunit.
source: Regulators of G-protein Signaling (RGS) are a family comprised of more than thirty proteins that share the eponymous and functionally conserved RGS domain; these proteins play a classical role in attenuating G protein-coupled receptor signaling through its GTPase-accelerating protein activity to inactivate the Gα subunit (Neubig and Siderovski, 2002; Keinan, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Neubig and Siderovski, 2002 and Keinan, 2014.

claim: RGS proteins can contribute to various cellular processes including cell differentiation.
source: RGS proteins are multifunctional proteins that can contribute to various cellular processes including cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about RGS proteins.

claim: Rgs12 is the largest protein in its family.
source: Rgs12 is unique in that it is the largest protein in its family.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Rgs12.

claim: Rgs12 contains a PSD-95/Dlg/ZO1 (PDZ) domain, a phosphotyrosine-binding (PTB) domain, a tandem Ras-binding domain (RBD1/2), and a GoLoco interaction motif in addition to the RGS domain.
source: In addition to the RGS domain, Rgs12 contains a PSD-95/Dlg/ZO1 (PDZ) domain, a phosphotyrosine-binding (PTB) domain, a tandem Ras-binding domain (RBD1/2), and a GoLoco interaction motif.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Rgs12 structure.

claim: The multi-domain architecture of Rgs12 is thought to facilitate its role as a scaffolding protein in complexes in which multiple signaling pathways might converge.
source: The multi-domain architecture of Rgs12 is thought to facilitate its role as a scaffolding protein in complexes in which multiple signaling pathways might converge (Snow et al., 2002; Sambi et al., 2006; Snow et al., 1998; Willard et al., 2007; Schiff et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: ROS are produced as a normal byproduct of cellular metabolism.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are produced as a normal byproduct of cellular metabolism (Callaway and Jiang, 2015) and forms the basis Denham Harman's free radical theory of aging, which perhaps is the most enduring model of aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Callaway and Jiang, 2015.

claim: Denham Harman's free radical theory of aging postulates that the gradual accumulation of damage inflicted by ROS eventually manifests as degenerative diseases associated with aging.
source: The theory of aging postulates that the gradual accumulation of damage inflicted by ROS eventually manifests as degenerative diseases associated with aging (Harman, 1956; Krause, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Harman, 1956 and Krause, 2007.

claim: ROS have been implicated in the management and prevention of cancers, cardiovascular diseases, macular degeneration, Alzheimer's disease, arthritis, and many other tissues.
source: In addition to longevity, ROS have been implicated in the management and prevention of cancers, cardiovascular diseases, macular degeneration, Alzheimer's disease, arthritis, and many other tissues—to which the bone is no exception (Naka et al., 2008; Domazetovic et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Naka et al., 2008 and Domazetovic et al., 2017.

claim: RANKL-induced ROS are indispensable for OC differentiation.
source: More recent studies have shown that RANKL-induced ROS are indispensable for OC differentiation (Callaway and Jiang, 2015; Lee et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2010; Bartell et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: ROS at low concentrations participate in signaling events in OCs, including the RANKL-dependent activation of mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs), phospholipase C gamma (PLCγ), nuclear factor kappa B (NFκB), and [Ca2+] oscillations.
source: At low concentrations, however, ROS have been shown to participate in signaling events in OCs, including the RANKL-dependent activation of mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs), phospholipase C gamma (PLCγ), nuclear factor kappa B (NFκB), and [Ca2+] oscillations; all of which contribute to the activation of nuclear factor of T-cells (NFAT), the master regulator of OC differentiation.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about ROS signaling in osteoclasts.

claim: NFAT is the master regulator of OC differentiation.
source: At low concentrations, however, ROS have been shown to participate in signaling events in OCs, including the RANKL-dependent activation of mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs), phospholipase C gamma (PLCγ), nuclear factor kappa B (NFκB), and [Ca2+] oscillations; all of which contribute to the activation of nuclear factor of T-cells (NFAT), the master regulator of OC differentiation.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about NFAT's role in osteoclast differentiation.

claim: Suppression of ROS by various means could inhibit OC differentiation.
source: Multiple lines of evidence have consistently shown that suppression of ROS by various means could inhibit OC differentiation (Lee et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2010; Bartell et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: RANKL-dependent activation of PLCγ, [Ca2+] oscillations, and NFAT were abrogated when OC precursors were treated with the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (NAC).
source: In particular, RANKL-dependent activation of PLCγ, [Ca2+] oscillations, and NFAT were abrogated when OC precursors were treated with the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (NAC) (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2010.

claim: Rgs12 silencing could inhibit PLCγ activation, [Ca2+] oscillations, and the expression of NFATc1 and its downstream factors.
source: Furthermore, our previous studies demonstrated that Rgs12 silencing could inhibit PLCγ activation, [Ca2+] oscillations, and the expression of NFATc1 and its downstream factors (Yang and Li, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yang and Li, 2007.

claim: Rgs12flox/flox mice crossed with LyzMCre transgenic mice generated Rgs12 cKO mice specific to the myeloid lineage.
source: To assess the role of Rgs12 in OC differentiation and bone remodeling in vivo, we generated a conditional gene knockout mouse model by crossing Rgs12flox/flox mice with Lysozyme M-cre (LyzMCre) transgenic mice (Rgs12 cKO).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data describing the mouse model generation.

claim: The LyzM promoter-driven Cre expression targets Rgs12 gene deletion to cells of the myeloid lineage, including monocytes/macrophages.
source: The LyzM promoter-driven Cre expression targets Rgs12 gene deletion to cells of the myeloid lineage, including monocytes/macrophages (Abram et al., 2014; Clausen et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Abram et al., 2014 and Clausen et al., 1999.

claim: Micro-CT analysis of the distal femurs obtained from Rgs12flox/flox and Rgs12+/+;LyzMCre showed no statistically difference in bone histomorphometry.
source: Micro-CT analysis of the distal femurs obtained from Rgs12flox/flox and Rgs12+/+;LyzMCre showed no statistically difference in bone histomorphometry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by micro-CT data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Cre-lox-mediated deletion of the Rgs12 gene was confirmed by PCR amplification of spleen genomic DNA.
source: The Cre-lox-mediated deletion of the Rgs12 gene was confirmed by PCR amplification of spleen genomic DNA (Figure 1A) and qPCR to measure Rgs12 transcripts in isolated bone marrow macrophages (BMMs) (Figure 1B), thereby confirming our mouse Rgs12 cKO model.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The Cre-lox-mediated deletion of the Rgs12 gene was confirmed by qPCR to measure Rgs12 transcripts in isolated bone marrow macrophages (BMMs).
source: The Cre-lox-mediated deletion of the Rgs12 gene was confirmed by PCR amplification of spleen genomic DNA (Figure 1A) and qPCR to measure Rgs12 transcripts in isolated bone marrow macrophages (BMMs) (Figure 1B), thereby confirming our mouse Rgs12 cKO model.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Rgs12 cKO mice exhibited increased trabecular bone mass, evident in the hematoxylin and eosin (H and E)-stained sections of the proximal tibia.
source: Rgs12 cKO mice exhibited increased trabecular bone mass, evident in the hematoxylin and eosin (H and E)-stained sections of the proximal tibia (Figure 1C) and 3D micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) visualization of the femoral trabecular bone morphology and microarchitecture (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Rgs12 cKO mice exhibited increased trabecular bone mass, evident in 3D micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) visualization of the femoral trabecular bone morphology and microarchitecture.
source: Rgs12 cKO mice exhibited increased trabecular bone mass, evident in the hematoxylin and eosin (H and E)-stained sections of the proximal tibia (Figure 1C) and 3D micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) visualization of the femoral trabecular bone morphology and microarchitecture (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by micro-CT data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Quantitative micro-CT measurements demonstrated statistically significant increases in bone volume (VOX-BV/TV) in Rgs12 cKO mice.
source: Quantitative micro-CT measurements further demonstrated statistically significant increases in bone volume (VOX-BV/TV), accompanied by increases in both trabecular number (Tb.N) and thickness (Tb.Th), and reduced trabecular separation (Tb.Sp) (Figure 1E–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative micro-CT data shown in Figure 1E-I.

claim: Quantitative micro-CT measurements demonstrated increases in both trabecular number (Tb.N) and thickness (Tb.Th) in Rgs12 cKO mice.
source: Quantitative micro-CT measurements further demonstrated statistically significant increases in bone volume (VOX-BV/TV), accompanied by increases in both trabecular number (Tb.N) and thickness (Tb.Th), and reduced trabecular separation (Tb.Sp) (Figure 1E–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative micro-CT data shown in Figure 1E-I.

claim: Quantitative micro-CT measurements demonstrated reduced trabecular separation (Tb.Sp) in Rgs12 cKO mice.
source: Quantitative micro-CT measurements further demonstrated statistically significant increases in bone volume (VOX-BV/TV), accompanied by increases in both trabecular number (Tb.N) and thickness (Tb.Th), and reduced trabecular separation (Tb.Sp) (Figure 1E–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative micro-CT data shown in Figure 1E-I.

claim: The targeted deletion of Rgs12 in mice resulted in increased bone mass.
source: Therefore, the targeted deletion of Rgs12 in mice resulted in increased bone mass.
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective micro-CT and histological data presented.

claim: There was no difference in osteoblast numbers between Rgs12 cKO and control bone tissues.
source: The histological assessment clearly demonstrates no difference in osteoblast numbers between Rgs12 cKO and control bone tissues (Figure 1K) whereas the number of TRAP+ multinucleated cells were markedly reduced in Rgs12-deficient samples (Figure 1L and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The number of TRAP+ multinucleated cells were markedly reduced in Rgs12-deficient samples.
source: The histological assessment clearly demonstrates no difference in osteoblast numbers between Rgs12 cKO and control bone tissues (Figure 1K) whereas the number of TRAP+ multinucleated cells were markedly reduced in Rgs12-deficient samples (Figure 1L and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by TRAP staining data shown in Figure 1L and M.

claim: The rate of bone formation was comparable between Rgs12 cKO and control mice.
source: Furthermore, a dynamic histomorphometric analysis by double calcein labeling to measure bone growth over time shows that the rate of bone formation was comparable between Rgs12 cKO and control mice (Figure 1N–P).
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamic histomorphometry data shown in Figure 1N-P.

claim: Rgs12 protein and transcript levels were dramatically upregulated upon stimulation by M-CSF and RANKL.
source: Rgs12 protein and transcript levels were dramatically upregulated upon stimulation by the differentiation factors, and seem to consistently increase into OC maturity at day 5 (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Rgs12-deficient precursor cells showed a reduction in the number of OCs containing 6–9 nuclei and 10+ nuclei.
source: A comparison of osteoclastogenic potential between precursors derived from Rgs12 cKO and control mice show that while control BMMs differentiated into large, TRAP+ multinucleated OCs, Rgs12-deficient precursor cells showed a reduction in the number of OCs containing 6–9 nuclei and 10+ nuclei, which were also visibly smaller (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TRAP staining and quantification data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Rgs12-deficient OCs were visibly smaller than control OCs.
source: A comparison of osteoclastogenic potential between precursors derived from Rgs12 cKO and control mice show that while control BMMs differentiated into large, TRAP+ multinucleated OCs, Rgs12-deficient precursor cells showed a reduction in the number of OCs containing 6–9 nuclei and 10+ nuclei, which were also visibly smaller (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TRAP staining data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Rgs12-deficient OCs have significantly reduced ability to resorb calcium phosphate surfaces.
source: We also probed into the overall bone resorptive activity and found that Rgs12-deficient OCs have significantly reduced ability to resorb calcium phosphate surfaces (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by bone resorption assay data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: The overexpression of Rgs12 in RAW264.7 cells led to an increased number of OCs with 10+ nuclei.
source: Contrasting our findings in Rgs12 cKO primary cells, we found that the overexpression of Rgs12 in RAW264.7 cells led to an increased number of OCs with 10+ nuclei (Figure 2H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by TRAP staining and quantification data shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: Rgs12 overexpression resulted in significantly decreased numbers of smaller OCs containing 3–5 and 6–9 nuclei.
source: We also observed significantly decreased numbers of smaller OCs containing 3–5 and 6–9 nuclei in Rgs12 overexpressing cells, presumably because most of the smaller OCs have fused to form large OCs containing 10+ nuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by TRAP staining and quantification data.

claim: A greater proportion of large OCs were active whereas non-resorbing OCs were on average smaller.
source: A previous study investigating the relationship between OC size and state of resorptive activity found that a greater proportion of large OCs were active whereas non-resorbing OCs were on average smaller (Lees et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lees et al., 2001.

claim: Rgs12-overexpressing OCs were significantly larger as compared to empty vector-transfected controls.
source: The quantification of the mean areas of OCs with 10+ nuclei revealed that Rgs12-overexpressing OCs were significantly larger as compared to empty vector-transfected controls (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Ectopic overexpression of Rgs12 in OCs potently increased bone resorption activity.
source: Consistent with our overall findings, ectopic overexpression of Rgs12 in OCs potently increased bone resorption activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by bone resorption assay data shown in Figure 2K-L.

claim: Proteomics analysis identified 3714 quantifiable proteins that are present in all samples.
source: Proteomics analysis identified 3714 quantifiable proteins that are present in all samples (no missing data), using a highly stringent identification criteria of ≥2 peptides per protein and 1% false discovery rate (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Within the proteomics dataset, 83 unique proteins were significantly upregulated in Rgs12 cKO OCs relative to control.
source: Within this dataset, we identified 83 and 61 unique proteins that were significantly up- and downregulated, respectively, in Rgs12 cKO OCs relative to control.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data analysis.

claim: Within the proteomics dataset, 61 unique proteins were significantly downregulated in Rgs12 cKO OCs relative to control.
source: Within this dataset, we identified 83 and 61 unique proteins that were significantly up- and downregulated, respectively, in Rgs12 cKO OCs relative to control.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data analysis.

claim: Most of the protein expression changes in Rgs12-deficient cells were captured at 3 and 5 days of OC differentiation.
source: Most of the protein expression changes in Rgs12-deficient cells were captured at 3 and 5 days of OC differentiation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The proteomic disturbances as a result of Rgs12 deletion closely coincided with the pattern of endogenous Rgs12 protein expression during OC differentiation.
source: Interestingly, the proteomic disturbances as a result of Rgs12 deletion closely coincided with the pattern of endogenous Rgs12 protein expression during OC differentiation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing proteomics data with Rgs12 expression data.

claim: OC marker proteins including metalloproteinase-9 (Mmp9), TRAP, ATPase H+ transporting V0 subunit D2 (Atp6v0d2), and integrin β3 (Itgb3) were significantly downregulated in Rgs12 cKO OCs.
source: Closer inspection showed that OC marker proteins including metalloproteinase-9 (Mmp9), TRAP, ATPase H+ transporting V0 subunit D2 (Atp6v0d2), and integrin β3 (Itgb3) were significantly downregulated in Rgs12 cKO OCs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Numerous Nrf2-dependent antioxidant enzymes were significantly upregulated in Rgs12 cKO OCs, including: peroxiredoxin 1/4 (Prdx1/4), thioredoxin 1/2 (Trxr1), glutathione reductase (Gshr), and NAD(P)H dehydrogenase quinone 1 (Nqo1).
source: Inspection of the proteins involved in these pathways showed a significant upregulation of numerous Nrf2-dependent antioxidant enzymes responsible attenuating oxidative stress, including: peroxiredoxin 1/4 (Prdx1/4), thioredoxin 1/2 (Trxr1), glutathione reductase (Gshr), and NAD(P)H dehydrogenase quinone 1 (Nqo1) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Upstream regulator analysis identified that the antioxidant enzymes upregulated in Rgs12 cKO OCs share the common upstream regulator Nrf2.
source: Upstream regulator (transcription factor) analysis by the Ingenuity Pathway Analysis software function identified that the antioxidant enzymes upregulated in Rgs12 cKO OCs share the common upstream regulator Nrf2, a key transcription factor that regulates cellular redox balance through the expression of protective antioxidant and phase II detoxification proteins. (Venugopal and Jaiswal, 1996; Itoh et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis and citations to Venugopal and Jaiswal, 1996 and Itoh et al., 1997.

claim: Nrf2 is a key transcription factor that regulates cellular redox balance through the expression of protective antioxidant and phase II detoxification proteins.
source: Upstream regulator (transcription factor) analysis by the Ingenuity Pathway Analysis software function identified that the antioxidant enzymes upregulated in Rgs12 cKO OCs share the common upstream regulator Nrf2, a key transcription factor that regulates cellular redox balance through the expression of protective antioxidant and phase II detoxification proteins. (Venugopal and Jaiswal, 1996; Itoh et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Venugopal and Jaiswal, 1996 and Itoh et al., 1997.

claim: Proteins of typically low abundance such as cytokines, signal regulatory molecules, and transcription factors tend to be 'crowded out' during MS analysis by more highly abundant proteins.
source: Proteins of typically low abundance such as cytokines, signal regulatory molecules, and transcription factors tend to be 'crowded out' during MS analysis by more highly abundant proteins such those proteins involved in glycolysis and purine metabolism, protein translation, and cytoskeletal components (Beck et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Beck et al., 2011.

claim: Western blotting of Nrf2 in day 3 OCs showed increased levels of Nrf2 in Rgs12 cKO cells.
source: Western blotting of Nrf2 in day 3 OCs also showed increased levels of Nrf2 in Rgs12 cKO cells (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Keap1 was elevated in Rgs12-deficient cells.
source: Keap1, however, which is known to suppresses Nrf2 activity by facilitating its degradation via the proteasome pathway, was unexpectedly elevated in Rgs12-deficient cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Keap1 suppresses Nrf2 activity by facilitating its degradation via the proteasome pathway.
source: Keap1, however, which is known to suppresses Nrf2 activity by facilitating its degradation via the proteasome pathway, was unexpectedly elevated in Rgs12-deficient cells.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Keap1's role.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining demonstrated increased nuclear translocation of Nrf2 in Rgs12 cKO cells.
source: Furthermore, immunofluorescence staining of Nrf2 demonstrated increased nuclear translocation of the transcription factor in Rgs12 cKO cells (Figure 4C, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The elimination of ROS with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was able to completely suppress Nrf2 nuclear translocation in both Rgs12 cKO and control BMMs.
source: The elimination of ROS with N-acetylcysteine (NAC), a precursor to the antioxidant glutathione, was able to completely suppress Nrf2 nuclear translocation in both Rgs12 cKO and control BMMs (Figure 4C, middle panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: NAC is a precursor to the antioxidant glutathione.
source: The elimination of ROS with N-acetylcysteine (NAC), a precursor to the antioxidant glutathione, was able to completely suppress Nrf2 nuclear translocation in both Rgs12 cKO and control BMMs (Figure 4C, middle panel).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about NAC.

claim: Induction of oxidative stress using the peroxide tert-buthylhydroxyperoxide (tBHP) potently induced Nrf2 nuclear translocation.
source: Conversely, induction of oxidative stress using the peroxide tert-buthylhydroxyperoxide (tBHP) potently induced Nrf2 nuclear translocation (Figure 4C, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The RANKL-dependent ROS induction observed in control cells was suppressed in Rgs12 cKO OCs.
source: As expected, the RANKL-dependent ROS induction observed in control cells was suppressed in Rgs12 cKO OCs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Under basal conditions, Nrf2 remains inactive through its interaction with Keap1, which causes its continual ubiquitination and degradation via the proteasome pathway.
source: Under basal conditions (i.e. absence of cellular stress), Nrf2 remains inactive through its interaction with Keap1, which causes its continual ubiquitination and degradation via the proteasome pathway (Stewart et al., 2003; Zhang and Hannink, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stewart et al., 2003 and Zhang and Hannink, 2003.

claim: A variety of stress conditions can induce conformational changes in Keap1, thereby releasing Nrf2 from the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, allowing it to accumulate and translocate into the nucleus.
source: A variety of stress conditions can induce conformational changes in Keap1, thereby releasing Nrf2 from the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, allowing it to accumulate and translocate into the nucleus (Itoh et al., 2003; Kensler et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Itoh et al., 2003 and Kensler et al., 2007.

claim: RAW264.7 cells overexpressing Rgs12 showed a significant reduction of Nrf2 protein levels that resulted from Keap1 inhibition compared to those in the control cells.
source: More importantly, RAW264.7 cells overexpressing Rgs12 showed a significant reduction of Nrf2 protein levels that resulted from Keap1 inhibition compared to those in the control cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The ability of Rgs12 to facilitate Nrf2 degradation despite the inhibition of Keap1 suggests that Rgs12 functions downstream of Keap1.
source: Moreover, the ability of Rgs12 to facilitate Nrf2 degradation despite the inhibition of Keap1 suggests that Rgs12 functions downstream of Keap1, either by controlling the ubiquitination or proteasomal degradation of Nrf2.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: tBHQ is a selective inhibitor of Keap1 activity by covalently binding the protein's reactive thiols.
source: tBHQ is a selective inhibitor of Keap1 activity by covalently binding the protein's reactive thiols and as a result activate Nrf2 and its downstream proteins in RAW264.7 cells (Abiko et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Abiko et al., 2011.

claim: tBHQ was previously shown to inhibit OC differentiation via the upregulation of heme oxygenase-1, a Nrf2-dependent antioxidant enzyme.
source: tBHQ was also previously shown to inhibit OC differentiation via the upregulation of heme oxygenase-1, a Nrf2-dependent antioxidant enzyme (Yamaguchi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yamaguchi et al., 2014.

claim: Rgs12 was still able to suppress Nrf2 despite the pharmacological blockade of Keap1 activity.
source: However, we observed that Rgs12 was still able to suppress Nrf2 despite the pharmacological blockade of Keap1 activity, thereby indicating that Rgs12 functions downstream of Keap1.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Inhibiting the proteasome was able to reverse the Rgs12-mediated degradation of Nrf2.
source: In fact, inhibiting the proteasome was able to reverse the ability of Rgs12 to promote Nrf2 degradation, indicating the requirement for Rgs12 in the proteasome's function.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: RANKL treatment correlated with reduced Nrf2 levels in OCs.
source: Interestingly, RANKL treatment correlated with reduced Nrf2 levels in OCs (Figure 5D, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: RANKL has a suppressive effect on Nrf2 expression, which was attributed to reduced transcriptional activity.
source: Our observation corroborates with previous findings documenting the suppressive effect of RANKL on Nrf2 expression, which was attributed to reduced transcriptional activity (Kanzaki et al., 2013; Hyeon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kanzaki et al., 2013 and Hyeon et al., 2013.
